ridge.title: A ridge, the setting Sun, and 12.7 arcminutes
ridge.mini: From a viewpoint at 1,690 m in the French Alps, Le Grand Mourre stands 208 m higher, 54 km away. A plane puts it 13′ above eye level, a globe puts it level. On 24 November 2026 the Sun sets behind it: a camera decides.
ridge.text: From a documented viewpoint at 1,690 m in the Alpes-de-Haute-Provence, Le Grand Mourre (1,898 m) stands 208 m higher, 54.1 km away [1]. On a plane only height counts, so a summit higher than you is above eye level at any distance: 13.2′. On a sphere of radius 6,371 km, curvature costs it 231 m over that range, more than its extra height: 1.4′ below eye level with straight rays, 0.5′ above with standard refraction (k = 0.13). The 12.7′ gap is 39 % of the solar disc, and the far ridge, traced on LiDAR terrain [2], keeps it across a 3° window. On 24 November 2026 the Sun sets into that window: first contact at 16:54:48 CET, upper limb gone at 16:58:17, for the standard atmosphere at the viewpoint [3][4]. Drawn at true angular scale, with no exaggeration.
ridge.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: the ridge photographed about 13′ above the Sun's centre at the stated minute, two fifths of a disc high.
crossing.title: Where two ridges touch
crossing.mini: Seen from 1,690 m, a ridge 16 km away and another 54 km away cross on the skyline. On a globe the corner sits 5.3′ below eye level; on a plane, 0.6′ above and 0.09° further right. A filtered Sun setting onto it shows which.
crossing.text: From the viewpoint, a near ridge 16 km away and a far ridge 54 km away meet on the skyline. The two points that touch lie on opposite sides of eye level: on the IGN's LiDAR the near one is 7 m below the observer, the far one 119 m above [1]. On a plane only height counts, so at that azimuth the two cannot appear at the same height, and the corner has to slide along the steep near ridge. The same terrain puts the corner at azimuth 241.29° and 5.3′ below eye level on a globe with standard refraction (241.27° and 6.2′ below with straight rays), and at 241.38°, 0.6′ above, on a plane: 0.09° apart sideways and 5.9′ vertically, a sixth and a fifth of the solar disc. The Sun of 24 November 2026 sets onto that corner [2]. The limit, stated plainly: the argument needs the observer's height to within a few metres, because the near margin is only 6 to 7 m.
crossing.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: the corner of the two ridges photographed at 241.38°, 0.6′ above eye level, rather than at 241.29°, 5.3′ below.
map.title: Where the Sun sets, on the flat-earth map
map.mini: On the map flat-earth sources publish, the Sun's direction is the straight line to the point it stands over. At sunset on 24 November 2026 that line misses the compass bearing by 32.7°, 61 solar diameters. Refraction cannot bend a direction.
map.text: The disc is the azimuthal-equidistant map flat-earth sources publish, north pole at the centre and Antarctica as the rim [1]. On a flat world the Sun stands over one point of it, fixed by the date and the clock alone, and its direction from the viewpoint is the straight line to that point, whatever the lamp's height. At sunset on 24 November 2026 that line points to 273.84°. The globe's bearing, the one a compass gives, is 241.15°, straight at the ridge where the Sun is predicted to set [2]. The two disagree by 32.7°, 61 solar diameters. Both are measured from local north, which on this map is the direction to the centre, so they can be compared. Refraction bends light vertically, so no atmosphere can close a gap in azimuth, and nothing is left to adjust. The great-circle arc is drawn for context only: the projection stretches east–west by about 12 % at this latitude, so no angle should be read off it.
map.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: the setting Sun found at a compass bearing near 274°, rather than near 241°.
dr.title: The one symbol a plane does not have
dr.mini: On a plane, the angle up to a summit depends only on its extra height and its distance. On a sphere the radius R enters too: the angle loses d/(2R), 14.6′ at 54 km. A plane has no size to compare a distance to.
dr.text: Three formulas carry the whole argument, and it turns on which symbols appear in them. On a plane, tan α = Δh/d: double the height difference and the distance and the angle does not change, because a plane has no length scale. On a sphere the target's vertical has swung by γ = d/R, and tan α = (r₂ cos γ − r₁)/(r₂ sin γ), with r = R + h. For small γ this is the plane's answer minus d/(2R), a term that exists only because R is finite. At 54.1 km it is 14.6′ with straight rays and 12.7′ with standard refraction, k = 0.13, which bends sight lines as if the radius were R/(1 − k). The middle panel draws the curvature ×90 by shrinking the planet at one scale for both axes, never by stretching an axis; the right-hand panel is at true scale.
dr.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: distant summits whose elevation angles follow Δh/d alone, with no deficit that grows with distance.
jan10.title: 10 January 2026: one sunset, four ways
jan10.mini: A camera on a tripod, aimed in advance at the notch where the globe's Sun should set. Beside its recording: the globe's prediction, the same Sun over a plane's higher ridge, and the flat model's own Sun, 23° up and never setting.
jan10.text: On 10 January 2026 a P900 camera on a tripod at the viewpoint was aimed in advance at the notch where the globe's Sun was due to set. Four panels share its direction, zoom and instant, at true angular scale on both axes. A, the globe: the ephemeris Sun [1] with standard refraction over the LiDAR ridge [2], first contact at 17:09:14 CET, gone at 17:13:10. B, the same Sun over a plane, whose far ridge stands higher: it would vanish earlier, from 17:08:10 to 17:11:29. C, the flat model's own Sun, a lamp 5,000 km above the point under the real Sun: about 33° to the right of the frame and 23° up, never setting. D, the camera's own recording, sped up ×20, which sets the clock for all six. E and F show the same instant from above: on the globe the great circle from the viewpoint runs to the point beneath the Sun; on the flat-earth map the Sun's bearing, laid off straight, misses it. A network clock filmed beside the camera's screen confirms its time to about a second.
jan10.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: the Sun in the recording gone at the plane's times, a minute early, or no Sun in the aimed frame at all.
jan10-video.title: The prediction beside the recording
jan10-video.mini: Left, where a globe puts the Sun and the ridge on 10 January 2026, computed in advance. Right, what the camera filmed at the same instant, sped up ×20. Its clock is confirmed by a network clock filmed in shot.
jan10-video.text: Left: the Sun of the ephemeris [1], with standard refraction, over the ridge as the LiDAR terrain [2] and a globe of radius 6,371 km place it, seen by a fixed camera at the viewpoint on 10 January 2026, at true angular scale: first contact at 17:09:14 CET, gone at 17:13:10. Right: the camera's own recording, same direction and zoom, sped up ×20 and run in step. On a plane the far ridge stands higher and the same Sun would be gone by 17:11:29; the flat model's own Sun would not be in the frame at all. The recording's time agrees to about a second with a network clock filmed beside the camera's screen.
jan10-video.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: the Sun in the recording gone at the plane's times, a minute early, or no Sun in the aimed frame at all.
